summary_html: **Mandatory reporters** (designated professionals) must report suspected child abuse or neglect. Federal law sets the funding and policy floor (CAPTA) and mandates reporter frameworks on federal lands/facilities (VICAA).
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — federal floor for state reporting systems  
- **Victims of Child Abuse Act (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — includes federal-facility reporter duties (recodified from former 42 U.S.C. §13031)

regulations_applicable.title: Vermont DCF Family Services Division rules and policy manual (Rule 2000 Response to Child Abuse and Neglect; Rule 3000 Administrative Review Process; Rule 7000 Transition Age Youth)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Willis S. Sheldon, Individually and as Administrator of the Estate of Dezirae Sheldon v. Nicholas Ruggiero
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for a DCF administrative reviewer was affirmed because the mandated-reporter duty under 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a) is triggered only by reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused, and a repetitious allegation adding nothing new did not supply it.
key_cases.relevance: Sheldon is Vermont's leading modern decision on when § 4913(a) actually obliges a mandated reporter to report, and it holds the trigger is reasonable cause to believe, judged on what the reporter newly learned.
key_cases.quote: In this context, as a matter of law, defendant did not have reasonable cause to make a report.

key_cases.case_name: LaShay v. Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services
key_cases.holding: A caseworker supervisor was not entitled to official immunity on a claim that he ignored warnings about a foster home where the child was later sexually abused, and SRS waived sovereign immunity to the extent of its liability insurance.
key_cases.relevance: LaShay holds that where reporting is mandatory it is a ministerial duty, so a Vermont official who fails to report cannot claim discretionary-act immunity.
key_cases.quote: Further, if reporting were mandatory, it was a ministerial, not a discretionary duty.

key_cases.holding: SRS (now DCF) owed the reporting children an actionable duty of care because 33 V.S.A. § 4915 imposes mandatory investigative acts for the protection of a particular class, and sovereign immunity did not bar the negligence suit.
key_cases.relevance: Sabia holds that the mandatory-investigation statute triggered by a report creates a duty running to the identified children, which is what gives a mandated report legal consequence in Vermont.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, we conclude that SRS had a duty to protect plaintiffs under the circumstances of this case.

search_keywords: Vermont Department for Children and Families

state_agency.name: Vermont Department for Children and Families, Family Services Division

mandatory_reporters: Health care providers, including physicians, surgeons, osteopaths, chiropractors, physician assistants, resident physicians, interns, hospital administrators, registered nurses, licensed practical nurses, medical examiners, emergency medical personnel, dentists, psychologists, and pharmacists — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(1)

School district and approved or recognized independent school employees, and contracted student-services providers, including superintendents, headmasters, teachers, student teachers, school librarians, principals, and guidance counselors — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(2)
Agency of Human Services employees, contractors, and grantees who have contact with clients — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(7)
Camp owners (“camp” includes any residential or nonresidential recreational program, 33 V.S.A. § 4913(b)) — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(9)
Members of the clergy, except information received while acting as a spiritual advisor in a confidential communication (33 V.S.A. § 4913(j)) — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(12)
Employees of the Office of the Child, Youth, and Family Advocate — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(13)
reporting_details: Vermont is not a universal-reporting state: the 13 categories of mandated reporters listed in 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a) must report to DCF within 24 hours of the time the information was first received or observed, and any other concerned person may report voluntarily (33 V.S.A. § 4913(c), (e)).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 72 hours to begin an assessment or investigation
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the report, once accepted as a valid allegation and there is sufficient information to proceed
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: The Commissioner may waive the 72-hour requirement only when necessary to locate the child or to ensure the safety of the child or social worker (33 V.S.A. § 4915(b)).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days (assessment track); no statutory deadline (investigation track)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: An assessment may be extended only upon written justification by the Department and not beyond 60 days total (33 V.S.A. § 4915a(b)); Vermont sets no completion deadline for the investigation track (33 V.S.A. § 4915b).
